He conveyed to her that Frank admired her exceedingly—that he considered her very handsome and very engaging; and, with so much altogether in his favour, she felt that she ought not to pronounce harshly upon him. As Mrs. Weston remarked, ‘Young people must all have their little fancies.’

Among his new acquaintances in Surry, one person was less indulgently inclined. On the whole, throughout the parishes of Donwell and Highbury, he was judged with much fairness; ample allowance was granted to the small extravagances of so good-looking a young man, who smiled so frequently and bowed with such grace. But among them was one mind whose censorious powers neither bow nor smile could disarm—Mr. Knightley. He heard the circumstance at Hartfield, and for a moment said nothing; but almost directly afterwards Emma heard him murmur to himself, above the newspaper in his hand, ‘Hum! precisely the idle, foolish fellow I supposed him.’ She was half disposed to take offence; a moment’s attention, however, satisfied her that he had spoken merely to ease his own feelings, with no design of provoking hers; so she allowed it to pass.

Though in one particular they brought unwelcome intelligence, Mr. and Mrs. Weston’s morning visit proved remarkably well timed in another. An occurrence during their stay at Hartfield made Emma desire their counsel; and, more fortunately still, the counsel they offered was exactly what she desired.

The occurrence was this:—The Coles had resided at Highbury for several years, and were very worthy people—kindly, generous, and without pretension; yet their birth was humble, they belonged to trade, and their gentility was but moderate. On first settling in the country they had lived suitably to their income, quietly, entertaining few people, and those at little expense. The last year or two, however, had considerably enlarged their resources: their establishment in town had become more profitable, and prosperity in general had attended them. Their ambitions grew with their riches; they wanted a larger house and felt a stronger inclination for society. They enlarged their dwelling, increased their servants, and augmented expenses of every description, until in fortune and manner of living they stood second only to Hartfield. Their fondness for company and their new dining-room led everybody to expect dinner-parties; several, principally for the unmarried gentlemen, had already been given. Emma could scarcely imagine their venturing to invite the established and first families—Donwell, Hartfield, or Randalls. Were they to do so, nothing should induce her to attend; and she regretted that her father’s well-known habits would render her refusal less significant than she wished.

Shall I be car-ri-ed up to heaven, on flower-filled beds of ease,

While others struggle for the prize, and cross the blood-y seas?

People considered him a marvelous reader. At church social gatherings he was invariably asked to read poetry. When he finished, the ladies would raise their hands and drop them helplessly into their laps, roll their eyes, and shake their heads, as though to say, ‘No words can describe it; it is too beautiful, TOO beautiful for this earthly world.’

Once the hymn was over, the Reverend Mr. Sprague became a human noticeboard, reading announcements of meetings and societies and other matters until the list seemed likely to continue to the end of time. This curious habit still survives in America, even in its cities, in this age when newspapers are everywhere. Often, the less reason there is for preserving an old custom, the more difficult it becomes to remove it.

The minister now began to pray. It was a fine, generous prayer, and a detailed one. He appealed on behalf of the church and its little children; the village’s other churches; the village itself; the county; the state; the state’s officials; the United States; the churches of the United States; Congress; the President; government officers; poor sailors battered by stormy seas; the oppressed millions suffering beneath European monarchies and Eastern tyrannies; those who possessed the light and the good news but lacked eyes to see and ears to hear; and the heathens on distant islands. He ended by asking that the words he was about to deliver might be graciously received and, like seeds planted in fertile earth, eventually produce a welcome harvest of goodness. Amen.

Dresses rustled as the standing congregation sat. The boy whose story is told here had taken no pleasure in the prayer; he had merely endured it, if he had managed even that. He had fidgeted throughout, unconsciously counting off its details. He was not listening, but he knew the territory well, along with the minister’s customary route across it. Whenever some little piece of new material was slipped in, his ear caught it and his entire being protested. He regarded additions as unfair and downright dishonest. During the prayer a fly had landed on the back of the pew ahead of him. It tormented him by calmly rubbing its hands together, wrapping its arms about its head and polishing it so fiercely that the head seemed almost to detach from the body, exposing the thin thread of neck; then scraping its wings with its back legs and smoothing them against its body as though they were coat-tails. It carried out its entire grooming routine with the peaceful assurance of a creature that knew itself perfectly safe.

It was a time of the greatest happiness and the greatest misery, of wisdom and foolishness, of faith and disbelief. It was a season of Light and a season of Darkness, a spring of hope and a winter of despair. Everything lay ahead of us, and nothing lay ahead of us. We were all heading straight for Heaven, and we were all heading straight in the opposite direction. In short, those days were so much like our own that some of the loudest public voices insisted they could be described only in extremes, whether for good or evil.

England had a king with a large jaw and a plain-faced queen. France also had a king with a large jaw, but its queen had a beautiful face. In both countries, the powerful men who guarded their rich rewards from the state were absolutely certain that the existing order would last forever.

The year was seventeen seventy-five. England was blessed with spiritual revelations in those fortunate days, just as it is in ours. Mrs. Southcott had recently reached her blessed twenty-fifth birthday. A private soldier in the Life Guards, claiming prophetic powers, had announced her glorious coming by declaring that plans were in place for London and Westminster to be swallowed up. Only twelve years had passed since the Cock-lane ghost had been put to rest after tapping out its messages, just as the spirits of this past year, showing a supernatural lack of imagination, had tapped out theirs. Meanwhile, some ordinary earthly messages had recently reached the English king and people from a congress of British subjects in America. Strange to say, these have turned out to matter more to humanity than any message yet delivered by the spiritual descendants of the Cock-lane ghost.

France, generally less fortunate in spiritual matters than her sister nation with the shield and trident, slid smoothly downhill, printing paper money and spending it. Guided by her Christian religious leaders, she also amused herself with such humane achievements as condemning a young man to have his hands cut off, his tongue pulled out with pincers, and his body burned alive. His crime was failing to kneel in the rain to honour a dirty procession of monks passing fifty or sixty yards away, within his sight. Quite probably, when this victim was executed, trees were already growing in the forests of France and Norway that Fate, acting as a woodsman, had marked for cutting. They would be felled and sawn into boards to build a certain movable frame equipped with a sack and a blade—a machine destined for a terrible place in history.
